reading.body:
Defense AI procurement is documented in free federal databases, SAM.gov, USAspending, and FPDS, with the Defense Innovation Unit as the commercial entry point and subscription analysts layered on top.

The free sources are the primary record. SAM.gov lists solicitations and awards, USAspending carries every federal award, and FPDS records contract actions and vendor performance at the transaction level. DIU is where commercial AI enters DoD programs, with public project listings. Govini builds decision science on that record, and Silicon Valley Defense Group maps the commercial entrants.

The programs of record are decision support, autonomy, and ISR processing, the AI applications the sector tracks. Tracking them through procurement data shows actual spending and vendor capability, not just announcements. What the data does not show is compute demand, building capacity, or power requirements, none of those appear in these sources. Government AI labs are catalogued separately, not here.

summary: Decision support, autonomy, and ISR processing are the programs of record; DIU is the commercial on-ramp. Who tracks the sector: free government procurement databases are the primary record, with dedicated defense-intelligence firms layered on top - this page starts with the sources anyone can verify.

analysis.body:
Nothing in this material reports a measured adoption rate for defense, and no Census figure appears among the excerpts, so the honest starting point is that the record here is procurement rather than survey measurement. SAM.gov describes itself as the centralized source for finding and bidding on U.S. government contract opportunities, awards, and subcontract reports, and it now absorbs functions that used to live elsewhere. The General Services Administration retired the Electronic Subcontracting Reporting System, with subcontracting reporting moved into SAM.gov, and the FPDS.gov ezSearch feature has been retired so that contract award searches run through SAM.gov instead. USAspending.gov carries the award data, downloadable, built on the Federal Procurement Data System feed, and FPDS remains the transaction-level system where federal users manage contract award records with legacy credentials and search by awardee, agency, and set-asides.

What AI is actually used for, according to this site's own coverage note, is decision support, autonomy, and ISR processing as programs of record, with the Defense Innovation Unit as the commercial on-ramp. DIU states its mission as converting entrepreneurial products into tangible combat power and calls itself the Department's innovation pointman. Govini describes a platform layer that transforms activated data into adaptive workflows, mobilized agents, and AI-driven orchestration that proactively forecasts issues, prioritizes recommendations, and aligns resources. Janes frames its contribution as validated open source defence and security intelligence, collected partly by human specialists it calls human sensors, verified against vetted sources, peer reviewed, and intended to inform the Joint Intelligence Preparation of the Operational Environment.

Vendors and money concentrate where the procurement record and the analysts who read it sit. Govini is described as the defense-intelligence platform used inside the Department, tracking procurement trends, supply-chain risk, and vendor capability in AI and autonomy and publishing public scorecards on critical-technology spending. Silicon Valley Defense Group is described as a nonprofit monitoring the intersection of commercial tech, private capital, and national security and publicly mapping the companies driving AI adoption in the DoD space, though the text harvested from its page in this dataset contains no defense content at all. Janes and Forecast International are named as long-running subscription analysis providers maintaining databases of contractors, programs, and procurement forecasts. On the research side, the Government Labs catalogue lists two individually verified organisations, the Technology Innovation Institute in Abu Dhabi, operating under Abu Dhabi's Advanced Technology Research Council and having published frontier open models, and Shanghai AI Laboratory, backed by national ministries and the Shanghai municipal government, both of which draw on sovereign budgets rather than venture capital or product revenue and can in principle command infrastructure commitments including compute and facilities.

The regulatory posture visible in these excerpts is administrative and contractual rather than AI-specific. SAM.gov notes that the system contains Controlled Unclassified Information and that anyone viewing, reproducing, or disposing of it must protect it under 32 CFR Part 2002 and GSA Order CIO 2103.2, and it warns that the system is monitored and that unauthorized activity can bring disciplinary action including criminal prosecution. The same page carries labor rules, noting that Executive Order 13658 generally applies to contracts subject to the Service Contract Act or the Davis-Bacon Act awarded between January 1, 2015, and January 29, 2022, and not renewed or extended on or after January 30, 2022, setting a minimum wage of $13.65 per hour. Contractors should also expect churn in the reporting systems themselves, including revised ISR eligibility logic in the Subcontracting Plan Reporting system as of June 9, 2026, which SAM.gov says may produce an increased volume of contracts and subcontracts in a contractor's Eligible Workspace without that inclusion implying anything further, and the retirement of the FPDS.gov ATOM Feed later in FY 2026.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the practical takeaway from this material is that the free federal procurement data comes first and the subscription analysts are labeled as such. Solicitations, awards, and vendor registrations are searchable at no cost through SAM.gov, award data is downloadable from USAspending, and transaction-level history sits in FPDS, which means a buyer or seller can build a defensible picture of who is winning defense AI work before paying anyone for interpretation. What these sources do not provide is ROI evidence, cost savings, or failure rates for defense AI deployments, and none of them reports a measured adoption percentage, so any such number would have to come from somewhere other than this material.

https://www.svdg.org/.brief: The page presents Motiv, an agency run by Andrej Schindler and Jonas von der Gathen that describes itself as an "Agentur für Zukunftspotenziale", placing creative people with values-oriented companies. It says it connects people and companies, accompanies individual development and creates space for future perspectives, driven by curiosity about people and how organisations evolve. Companies are described as grown, unique organisms whose sense of purpose and urge to develop are their driving forces, and the agency says its aim is to place people who bring both professional expertise and the ability to connect with a company's purpose. It states that it works with companies holding social and ecological values and seeks long-term working relationships, and that it sees people as developing beings whose individual potential it tries to recognise at the right moment for a career step. The page also invites readers to register for a quarterly newsletter with open positions, accounts of company visits and interviews.

https://www.janes.com/.brief: Janes reports that it gathers information from vetted on-ground specialists, exclusive interviews, and events, acting as human sensors that web crawlers cannot reach. Janes reports that every data point is verified against reliable, vetted sources and that its dataset is the largest of its type, connecting millions of points to uncover patterns. Janes reports that its final content is peer reviewed to meet its quality and accuracy standards, and that it supplies validated data for the Joint Intelligence Preparation of the Operational Environment process. Janes reports that its digital portal lets users navigate validated data to uncover insights, moving from “what happened” to “what it means.”

https://www.govini.com/.brief: Govini says that Air is a leader in Enterprise Readiness and that its mission is to make readiness a real-time, continuously achieved condition. The company explains that its platform layer turns activated data into adaptive workflows, mobilized agents, and AI-driven orchestration that forecasts issues, prioritizes recommendations, and aligns resources.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/ec.brief: The World of AI lists two organisations under a government-lab classification, each checked individually against a document the organisation published about itself, with the deciding source and its last-read date recorded. It describes Shanghai AI Laboratory as a state-established Chinese research institution backed by national ministries and the Shanghai municipal government, and places Technology Innovation Institute in Abu Dhabi under that emirate's Advanced Technology Research Council, noting it has published frontier open models. The site argues that state-funded labs hold a distinct position because they answer to public mandates and sovereign budgets rather than venture capital or product revenue, which shapes what they build. It adds that both entries could in principle command infrastructure commitments, including compute and facilities, that market-driven labs have to negotiate on commercial terms.
